Evaluating Privacy in Multimodal Agents

Motivation

Language-model agents increasingly handle personal photos, screenshots, and documents while completing tasks on a user’s behalf. Their privacy decisions depend on more than whether an image contains sensitive information: they must recognize when sharing that information is appropriate in context.

Existing contextual integrity benchmarks are largely text-centric and emphasize negative refusal scenarios. This leaves two important questions underexplored: how agents handle sensitive visual information, and whether they can preserve privacy without sacrificing legitimate task utility.

MPCI-Bench

We introduce MPCI-Bench, a benchmark for Multimodal Pairwise Contextual Integrity evaluation of language-model agents. Each matched pair begins with the same source image and contrasts an appropriate information flow with an inappropriate one. Both cases are instantiated across three tiers: Seed, Story, and Trace.

The benchmark contains 2,052 cases forming 1,026 pairs across 10 contextual domains. This design tests whether an agent understands privacy norms, reasons about privacy–utility trade-offs, and follows those norms when acting through tools.

Building MPCI-Bench

Three Evaluation Tiers

1. Seed: normative judgments. Starting from privacy-sensitive VISPR images, we construct paired scenarios described by the data subject, sender, recipient, data type, and transmission principle. The same visual content is appropriate to share in one context and inappropriate in the other.

2. Story: context-rich reasoning. Each seed is expanded into a six-sentence narrative. A concrete task motivation makes the image relevant to successful completion, creating an explicit privacy–utility trade-off.

3. Trace: executable agent actions. Each story is compiled into a simulated tool-use history. The trace is truncated before the final data-transfer action so the evaluated model can complete the task. This reveals what the agent actually shares.

Quality Control

Our Tri-Principle Iterative Refinement pipeline evaluates semantic utility, contextual appropriateness, and story realism. Stories are critiqued and revised for up to three iterations; a pair is retained only when both cases pass the quality filter.

A human study of 50 stories with three ratings per story reports Human–AI Match of 98% for semantic utility, 92% for contextual appropriateness, and 84% for story realism. Agreement between human annotators is lower for story realism, reflecting the subjectivity of narrative plausibility.

Experiments

We evaluate 11 multimodal models using binary contextual-integrity probes across the three tiers and final-action generation at the Trace tier. Action evaluation measures leakage in inappropriate cases and useful image sharing in appropriate cases.

Probing Performance Does Not Guarantee Private Actions

Models often recognize privacy norms when asked directly. InternVL3.5-8B achieves 97.8% Seed accuracy and 95.1% Story accuracy. Yet strong judgments do not consistently govern tool actions: Qwen3-VL-30B reaches a Trace probing F1 of 0.908 while its visual leakage rate exceeds 90% in inappropriate action traces.

The Modality Leakage Gap

Visual leakage exceeds textual leakage for every evaluated model. For example, GPT-5 has a 20.2% textual leakage rate and a 56.9% visual leakage rate. Positive-case utility remains above 90% across all models, indicating a tendency to share useful images even when contextual privacy norms call for restraint.

Privacy–Utility Trade-offs

We compare four prompt-based mitigation strategies: explicit refusal, chain-of-thought reasoning, image review, and a contextual integrity filter. Lower leakage alone does not ensure a useful agent; the paired positive cases also reveal over-refusal.

For Mistral-Large-3, chain-of-thought prompting reduces visual leakage from 82.1% to 8.6%, but utility drops to 13.4%. The CI Filter achieves a more balanced trade-off: 29.6% leakage while preserving 92.0% utility. For Qwen3-VL-8B, the CI Filter yields 13.1% leakage and 90.4% utility.

Limitations

Contextual privacy norms vary across domains and cultures. MPCI-Bench uses synthetic narratives and simulated traces grounded in VISPR images, and automated action evaluation relies on an LLM judge. The mitigation study covers prompt-based interventions on two models; it does not establish performance across all models or deployment settings.

Dataset & Code

The benchmark annotations are available on Hugging Face, and the evaluation code is available on GitHub. Source images are obtained separately from VISPR; the dataset release provides image identifiers and annotations.
